props.title: Something New
props.initialSlug: Black professional woman dates white landscape architect

sections.content: Something New marked a refreshing shift in romantic comedy by directly addressing interracial relationships and class dynamics through a Black female protagonist's perspective. Sanaa Lathan stars as Kenya McQueen, a high-powered investment banker whose unexpected romance with white landscape architect Brian Kelly (Simon Baker) challenges her preconceptions. The film joins other groundbreaking 2000s romantic comedies like Save the Last Dance (2001) and Guess Who (2005) in examining interracial relationships, but stands out for centering a successful Black woman's experience without compromising her character's professional achievements or cultural identity.

sections.content: Director Sanaa Hamri's thoughtful handling of workplace microaggressions and family expectations elevates Something New beyond typical rom-com territory. The film's exploration of code-switching and Black upper-middle-class life preceded later works like Think Like a Man (2012) and The Best Man Holiday (2013). Its honest portrayal of Kenya's internal conflict between cultural loyalty and personal happiness resonated with audiences and critics, opening doors for more nuanced Black romantic leads.

The film's visual style deserves special attention, particularly in scenes contrasting Kenya's structured corporate world with Brian's organic garden designs. This aesthetic choice echoes similar environmental metaphors in films like Notting Hill (1999) and Garden State (2004), but with added layers of racial and cultural significance. The garden becomes a powerful symbol of growth and breaking free from self-imposed limitations. SUBHEAD: Impact on Modern Romance Films

sections.content: Something New helped pave the way for more diverse romantic narratives in Hollywood, influencing films like The Big Sick (2017) and Crazy Rich Asians (2018). Its success demonstrated audience appetite for love stories that don't shy away from cultural complexity while maintaining the warmth and charm of classic romantic comedies. The film's legacy can be seen in recent works like Always Be My Maybe (2019) and To All the Boys I've Loved Before (2018), which continue to expand representation in the genre.
